findings.title: Backup code entropy is only 40 bits per code
findings.body: Each backup code is generated as `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")`, producing a 10-character hex string with only 40 bits of entropy. Modern guidance (NIST SP 800-63B) recommends at least 64 bits of entropy for OTP secrets, and 128 bits is common. Because the code is the only thing standing between an attacker and account access (it bypasses the TOTP factor), 40 bits is brute-forceable in a realistic timeframe, especially since failed attempts do not consume the code and the API has no per-user rate limiting on the credentials provider beyond the existing email-based limiter.

findings.title: Backup code is not consumed on failed attempt; timing-unsafe comparison
findings.body: Two problems compound here: (1) `Array.prototype.indexOf` is not a constant-time comparison, so the time taken to find (or not find) a user-supplied backup code leaks information about how many leading bytes matched, enabling a timing side-channel that lets an attacker enumerate codes character by character. Use a constant-time comparison (e.g. compare each code with `crypto.timingSafeEqual` after length-checking). (2) The supplied code is only removed from the array after a successful match (`backupCodes[index] = null`), so failed attempts leave all 10 codes intact. Combined with the 40-bit entropy per code, this makes online brute force feasible: an attacker can submit unlimited guesses until one matches.

findings.title: Timing-unsafe backup code comparison and missing password for non-CAL users
findings.body: Same `backupCodes.indexOf(...)` timing leak as in the credentials provider: a constant-time comparison should be used. More importantly, the password check at line 40 is gated on `user.password && user.identityProvider === IdentityProvider.CAL`, so for SAML/Google users the only thing required to disable 2FA is a single valid backup code. A leaked backup code therefore gives an attacker the ability to log in via the credentials provider and then turn off 2FA entirely, reducing the account to a single factor. The credentials provider should still demand something only the legitimate user possesses (e.g. re-prompt for password, or require the SAML/Google re-authentication) before 2FA can be disabled.

findings.title: Default export is named TwoFactor, not BackupCode
findings.body: The file is `BackupCode.tsx` and consumers import it as `import BackupCode from "@components/auth/BackupCode"`, but the default export is declared as `export default function TwoFactor({ center = true })`. The mismatch is not a runtime error (default exports are not name-checked), but it is a clear copy/paste leftover that will confuse anyone reading the file or refactoring the codebase. Rename the function (and the display name / `displayName`) to `BackupCode`.

findings.title: Label is not associated with the input
findings.body: The `<Label>` renders `{t("backup_code")}` but has no `htmlFor` attribute, so screen readers do not announce it as the label for the backup-code input. Either pass an `htmlFor` matching the `id="backup-code"` on the `TextField`, or wrap the input with the label. The same `Label` import in `TwoFactor.tsx` has the same gap, so the new component was modeled on the existing bug.

findings.title: Object URL for backup-codes download is never revoked on unmount
findings.body: `URL.createObjectURL(textBlob)` is called whenever a user runs the setup, and the previous URL is revoked on the next setup, but the URL is not revoked when the component unmounts, when the modal is closed via the X / overlay, or when `onOpenChange(false)` fires. `resetState()` clears the state but does not call `URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl)`. The blob stays in memory for the lifetime of the page, which is both a memory leak and a minor data exposure concern (the plaintext backup codes are still in the page's blob store). Revoke the URL in a cleanup effect and in `resetState`.

findings.title: Backup-codes dialog buttons default to type="submit" and submit the TOTP form
findings.body: The Close, Copy, and Download buttons inside the `<WithStep step={SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes}>` block do not specify a `type` attribute, so they default to `type="submit"`. They are rendered inside the `<Form handleSubmit={handleEnable} form={form}>` which targets the TOTP form. The `e.preventDefault()` call in each onClick does stop the default for that click, but: (a) the auto-submit effect (line 157-161) watches `totpCode`, so the moment a user pastes or types in the TOTP boxes on the same screen the form will submit; (b) relying on `preventDefault` on a submit button is fragile and a maintenance trap. Add `type="button"` to all three buttons (and to the `Continue` button at line 247, which has the same issue but at least is inside a different WithStep so is less likely to fire today).

findings.title: formatBackupCode is used before it is declared
findings.body: `handleSetup` (line 77) calls `formatBackupCode` at line 95, but `formatBackupCode` is declared with `const` at line 163, after `handleSetup` in the source. The const is in the temporal dead zone until the component body finishes executing, so any path that reaches the use before mount (e.g. an early return, a future refactor that calls `handleSetup` during render, or a test that calls the function directly) will throw `ReferenceError: Cannot access 'formatBackupCode' before initialization`. It works today only because the user has to click the button after mount. Move the helper above `handleSetup` (or extract it to module scope) so the dependency order matches the source order.

findings.title: No e2e test covers backup-code login or backup-code disable
findings.body: The new backup-codes test only exercises the display/copy/download UI on the setup flow. There is no test for the actual auth-critical paths the PR introduces: (1) logging in with a backup code after clicking "Lost access", (2) the login path when the backup code is wrong (expect `incorrect_backup_code`), (3) disabling 2FA using a backup code from the settings modal. The author flagged this in the TODO on line 12, but these are the security-relevant paths and should not ship untested. In particular there is no regression coverage for the credential flow that consumes a code and re-encrypts the array.

findings.title: Download link is a plain <a> with no rel or sandboxing
findings.body: The "Download" button is wrapped in `<a download="cal-backup-codes.txt" href={backupCodesUrl}>` with no `rel="noopener"` or `type` attribute. While `download` is set so navigation is not expected, an `href` that is a `blob:` URL still benefits from the standard hardening, and a future change that switches to a same-origin URL would silently introduce a tabnabbing vector. Add `rel="noopener noreferrer"` to be safe.
